The Amur goby Rhinogobius giurinus reaches a maximum total length of 12.1 centimeters [Li = 12.1 centimeters] in its native range, a size that places it among the larger members of its genus. Field surveys of adult populations in Yangtze River tributaries have documented that individuals typically attain this ultimate dimension only after several growing seasons, reflecting a life history strategy that prioritizes gradual somatic expansion. The species demonstrates a clear size threshold for the onset of gonadal activity, with puberty occurring at a total length of 4.7 centimeters [Lp = 4.7 centimeters]. This relatively small size at maturation allows individuals to begin their reproductive contribution well before reaching full somatic size, a pattern common among small-bodied gobiids that face high predation pressure. Comparative data from congeneric species such as Rhinogobius brunneus suggest that once this length is achieved, the gonads undergo rapid recrudescence in response to lengthening photoperiods and rising water temperatures. The relationship between length and mass in this species is well described by the length-weight equation derived from large sample sizes, providing a reliable basis for estimating body condition across different populations and habitats.

Eggs of the Amur goby hatch after an incubation period of 8 days [ab = 8 days] when maintained at a precise incubation temperature of 22.420 °C [T = 22.420 °C], a duration that is relatively short compared to many freshwater teleosts. This rapid embryonic development is characteristic of species that deposit their adhesive eggs in shallow, well-oxygenated waters where thermal fluctuations are minimal. The newly emergent yolk-sac larvae are extremely small, with a wet weight at birth of just 0.0012 grams [Wwb = 0.0012 grams], reflecting the modest size of the fertilized ovum. Based on morphometric data from the closely related Rhinogobius brunneus, these eggs measure approximately 2.75 millimeters in length and 0.9 millimeters in width, placing them within the typical range for demersal-spawning gobies. The prolarvae remain in an endotrophic state for several days following eclosion, subsisting entirely on their yolk reserves before the mouth opens and the onset of exogenous feeding begins. This brief lecithotrophic phase is a critical window during which larval survival depends heavily on the energetic reserves provisioned by the female.

At a stable water temperature of 22.4 °C [T = 22.4 °C], spawning females of the Amur goby produce an average of 1,700 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 1,700 eggs per clutch] and typically deposit between four and five clutches annually [F_R_i = between four and five clutches annually]. This reproductive output translates into a substantial annual fecundity that allows the species to maintain stable populations despite considerable egg mortality from fungal infection and predation by benthic invertebrates. The thermal regime appears to be close to the optimal temperature for both gametogenesis and spawning behavior, with field observations noting that reproductive activity peaks when water temperatures stabilize near this value during the late spring and early summer months. Males establish nesting territories beneath stones or within crevices and vigorously defend the adhesive egg masses until hatching, a parental investment that increases the probability of successful embryonic development in the structurally complex littoral zones these fish inhabit.

The wet weight at puberty for the Amur goby is approximately 1.1 grams [Wwp = approximately 1.1 grams], a modest body mass that is reached when individuals attain the total length of 4.7 centimeters. This mass threshold marks the transition from a purely somatic growth phase to one that includes the energetic demands of reproduction. Upon reaching sexual maturity, the gonadosomatic index rises sharply as females begin vitellogenesis and males initiate spermatogenesis. Sexual maturity is attained at approximately 365 days after hatching [tp = 365 days after hatching]. The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults is 19.7 grams [Wwi = 19.7 grams], corresponding closely to the maximum recorded total length of 12.1 centimeters. This asymptotic mass represents the upper limit of body size achievable under natural conditions and is presumably constrained by both the energetic costs of foraging and the physical limitations of the benthic habitat. Comparisons with other Rhinogobius species indicate that this maximum mass is intermediate within the genus, reflecting a life history strategy that balances early reproduction with continued somatic investment. The maximum daily reproduction rate, calculated from these values, is approximately 4.7 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 4.7 eggs per day].

Longevity records for the Amur goby indicate a maximum lifespan of 730 days [am = 730 days] when maintained at a constant water temperature of 22.4 °C [T = 22.4 °C], a duration consistent with estimates from the sand goby Pomatoschistus minutus, a species that shares similar ecological traits. First reproduction is achieved at approximately 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], allowing even short-lived individuals to contribute at least one successful spawning event to the next generation. Under field conditions, few individuals survive beyond their second breeding season due to the cumulative physiological costs of reproduction and natural mortality from piscivorous predators. This compressed life history is well suited to the dynamic and often unpredictable freshwater environments that the species colonizes across its extensive East Asian distribution.
